Florian Wirtz admitted he has been unhappy with some of his performances for Liverpool but he is now enjoying being in his best run of form since joining the club.

The Germany playmaker’s performances have been intensely scrutinised since his £116m move from Bayer Leverkusen two summers ago and, after an underwhelming first season in a campaign where the whole team struggled, he has started to kick into gear.

He has scored five times and contributed two assists in his last four appearances for club and country and the smile is back on his face.

“In the last few games I got a lot of goal contributions and I think you could say that I am in the best form since I arrived,” he mentioned ahead of the Champions League game against Club Brugge in Belgium.

“To be honest, I cannot really say that I have changed much. I think that I have become a bit better on a physical level, that is the only reason I could explain it.

“But I also started to know better English football and the league and I am feeling very good. I am enjoying my football at Liverpool. I am happy it is going like this at the moment.

Sources indicate that “I have heard a lot of people talking about me smiling or that I don’t smile that much. Maybe that is only because the people don’t really know me. Normally I am a very positive guy.

“It’s just when I am on the pitch I try and bring out my best performances and be as focused as I can be. Maybe that is sometimes why it looks like I don’t smile so much, but I don’t think that is a thing you have to be concerned about.

It has been revealed that “It’s mainly a thing that goes on in my own head. It’s not about the people who talk about me. It’s the goals I set myself and the performances I want to show for myself.

In a recent development, “I always believed in myself. I knew my qualities and I know them now.

“Of course, there were days where I wasn’t happy with myself but I still believe it makes no sense to put too much pressure on yourself as that doesn’t help to get to where you want.

Industry observers note that “I just believed in myself so I wasn’t too annoyed. But now I can only speak about the time I am having now and I’m really enjoying it.”.

After a run one goal in 17 club appearances stretching back to May, the 23-year-old has scored in back-to-back matches and he created 10 chances in Sunday’s win against Manchester United, including an assist for Victor Munoz’s goal.

Wirtz added: “I would say my priority is that the club and the team is successful, that’s the main thing in my head.

“I know that offensive players get checked by numbers and I’m always trying to use my opportunities when I have them but, in the end, for me it’s just about the success of the team.

“I’m not going into a game and trying to be the player who has scored the most goals or something. If I see a team-mate in a better position I give them the ball and I hope they also do that with me.”.

#106057. Who did figure 3? Why scientists should make experimental contributions visible

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Who did figure 3? Why scientists should make experimental contributions visible

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Highlighting who was responsible for each experiment could be a boost to many researchers’ careers.Credit: miniseries/Getty.
  • According to recent reports, I ask this question surprisingly often when reading the literature.
  • In a recent development, after years of working in experimental cell biology, collaborating with other laboratories, reviewing papers and handling manuscripts as an editor, I have come to recognize that this is more than an inconvenience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Highlighting who was responsible for each experiment could be a boost to many researchers’ careers.Credit: miniseries/Getty.

According to recent reports, I ask this question surprisingly often when reading the literature. I might be interested in a particular imaging approach, trying to understand an experiment in detail when reviewing a manuscript or simply want to contact a study author who has experience with a technique. I look at the author list, then the contribution statement, and reach the same conclusion: I have no idea who did the work.

In a recent development, after years of working in experimental cell biology, collaborating with other laboratories, reviewing papers and handling manuscripts as an editor, I have come to recognize that this is more than an inconvenience. By obscuring who does what in a research project, we are losing an important piece of information about how science is done — and the people who do it.

Digital badges aim to clear up politics of authorship.

Digital badges aim to clear up politics of authorship.

This has become particularly obvious to me as my research has become more collaborative. My projects can involve advanced microscopy, molecular biology, animal experiments and computational analysis, each performed by a different group. This is one of the things I enjoy most about modern science: collaborations allow us to answer questions that none of us could address alone. But they also make individual expertise increasingly difficult to see.

Sources indicate that when I started in research 20 years ago, papers generally had fewer authors and the experimental work was performed in one or two laboratories. Today, papers routinely have 10, 20 or more authors, with projects spread across several institutes. A 2024 study1 in Scientometrics found that the mean number of authors on papers in the PubMed database grew by more than 50% between 2000 and 2020 (from 3.99 to 6.25). Author-contribution statements help to delineate individual roles in a project, but only to a point. If five people are listed under investigation, three under methodology and four under analysis, I still cannot tell who performed any one experiment.

Anyone who has spent time at the bench knows that experiments require more than simply following the methods section of a paper.

Industry observers note that I have seen young researchers spend months, sometimes years, developing expertise in a technique. When the resulting study is published through a large collaboration, that researcher might become one name among many, credited with investigation or methodology. But those words do not tell the person reading the paper that this is the scientist who knows how this experiment works.

It has been revealed that for early-career researchers, that’s a missed opportunity. Publications are not only records of scientific findings, they also demonstrate technical proficiency. Being able to say, “I am an author on this paper”, is valuable. Being identifiable as the person who generated a particular piece of evidence provides a different and, in some circumstances, more useful form of recognition.

Recent findings suggest that and there’s another benefit. As a reviewer and editor, I sometimes have technical questions. The corresponding author is, appropriately, my point of contact. But they might not be the person who performed or directly supervised the experiment I care about and, over time, they might not remember who did. PhD students graduate, postdocs change institutions and collaborations evolve. Five years after publication, identifying the person who remembers exactly how an experiment was performed can be difficult.

Industry observers note that we rightly devote enormous attention to reproducibility. We record catalogue numbers for antibodies, identify instruments and software versions and deposit raw data sets. Yet we often fail to record something much simpler: who generated the data. I am not suggesting this as a way of assigning blame when something goes wrong — authorship implies collective responsibility for a published study. I see it instead as a strategy to provide traceability of expertise.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03542-w.

#106056. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1594 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.
  • Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.
  • The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

According to recent reports, the youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very swiftly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”.

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

According to recent reports, mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

In a recent development, mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he stated.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”.

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

Sources indicate that the historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most key day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

According to recent reports, “Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”.

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

Industry observers note that A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

Rory McIlroy: I will win the Masters.

It has been revealed that at 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change swiftly at Augusta National.

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.
  • This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.
  • But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

It has been revealed that while the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

Sources indicate that "Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow.".

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off.

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

It has been revealed that so far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

Recent findings suggest that an unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

It has been revealed that even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he claims.

It has been revealed that indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football.".

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

Sources indicate that "I want to get away from this east-west debate," notes Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR.".

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

It has been revealed that "The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act.".

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition.".

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option.".

Recent findings suggest that support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion.".

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:.

Suddenly, the four newly introduced leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

Recent findings suggest that "The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future.".

The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that.".

Sources indicate that for Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

According to recent reports, this season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!".

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

"[The concern] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent.".

Industry observers note that any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he indicates before heading out for training.

According to recent reports, "It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth, something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary.

Sources indicate that voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space.

Sources indicate that "I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker stated during Thursday's event.

While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the issue, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon.

Recent findings suggest that "We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd said. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We at the moment don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently.".

"But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low.".

Sources indicate that according to Dodd, this anomaly isn't a major cause for long-term concern. Rather, it's likely just part of the natural aging process for spacecraft.

"These spacecraft are old," she stated. "All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know, sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things, and so we are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager just due to the distance and the age.".

"But we feel Voyager 1, although it's not sending us the telemetry data, it's pointed at the Earth. It's sending us a strong carrier signal, and I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back.".

Industry observers note that and, for anyone curious how Voyager 1's slower twin Voyager 2 is faring, Dodd shared that it is doing very well on its own journey through interstellar space. "Voyager 2 is very healthy. It's continuing its mission. It has three scientific instruments on it," she told Space.com.

"Each spacecraft is basically setting a record every day for longevity or distance," Dodd added about the twin probes.

Despite the communications anomaly — and even though most of the team had been up all night to confirm the one-light-day signal from Voyager 1 — the room was alive with excitement. The Voyagers have been flying for nearly 50 years on a mission expected to last just five years, so the team was beyond ready to celebrate.

In a recent development, amidst the more technical updates about the mission and its current status out in interstellar space, the event included footage of Voyager light-day celebrations from around the world. From children cheering on Voyager to iconic landmarks lighting up gold in honor of the mission's Golden Record, the Voyager love echoed around the world in photos and videos. The footage of this international celebration was enough to move Nicky Fox, NASA's associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate, nearly to tears.

"I actually thought I was going to start sobbing," Fox joked to Space.com after the media briefing. "I think just hearing children's voices and people saying 'We love you, Voyager,' 'Go Voyager' — it just was amazing.".

And Fox and the mission team members weren't the only ones sharing their love for Voyager. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins beamed down her own video message to the Voyager 1 spacecraft from the International Space Station, sharing in the celebration.

Recent findings suggest that "Dear Voyager 1," Watkins said. "As an orbiting outpost just 250 miles [400 kilometers] above Earth, we often feel distant yet deeply connected to our home planet. The International Space Station has had crew continuously living off of the Earth for 26 years, seen hundreds of visitors from around the world, and enabled thousands of experiments to advance space exploration.

In a recent development, "While you have been traveling into the unknown for nearly half a century, helping pave our path, together, our two journeys tell a single story of exploration," she continued. "One remains close to home, and the other reaches ever outward. Voyager 1, you have been a beacon of light, a symbol of exploration, a seeker of truth, a carrier of hope, a brave explorer, traveling further than any human hand has ever reached. You represent the very best of what humanity has to offer.

"As you reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the entire crew of Expedition 75 and people across the planet send you our admiration and our wishes for a safe and continued journey as you begin your post-one-light-day era. There are so many amazing milestones and discoveries to come. You have a universe ahead of you, and you carry with you our collective hopes and dreams. When we look up from Earth, we will always think of you as you continue forward into the great unknown. May you continue shining bright for all of us. Go Voyager 1!" Watkins noted, ending her message with a weightless backflip from aboard the station.

In concluding the media briefing, the mission team invited those in the room who, over the past 50 years (or more, with one person sharing their excitement having worked on Voyager before it was even called Voyager) have worked on the mission in one way or another, to stand up to a round of applause. With mission team members today ranging from those in their 20s to their 90s, the people behind this enduring mission span many generations.

Interestingly, Fox actually began her light-day celebrations earlier in the week. She, alongside writer/producer Ann Druyan — who was the wife of the late astronomer Carl Sagan, whose work helped create the mission's Golden Record and who took the now-famous "pale blue dot" Voyager image of Earth to the public — together lit up the Empire State Building gold.

In a recent development, "I was actually very privileged to flick the switch and turn on the Empire State Building lights on Tuesday evening [Nov. 17]," Fox, wearing golden Voyager-inspired nail polish crafted by her daughter, told Space.com. "That was just spectacular … I was there with Ann … we were both so giddy with the excitement of doing it … It was amazing. And then going up and standing underneath and seeing the tower was just really, really special.".

It has been revealed that while the room lit up with excitement for Voyager's light-day milestone on Thursday, the team was also brimming with anticipation for what lies ahead. As Voyager hurtles toward another major milestone, turning 50 in 2027, it remains an active science mission, and the team remains hard at work to push the boundaries of exploration with these aging probes.

Sources indicate that "Voyager right now — the two Voyagers — they're in an area of space that we've never been into. So every single bit of data that comes back is precious because it's unique," Fox stated.

"Now we're in a region where the sun's influence is a lot different, and we're in this region where we can start to understand: What is it like out past our sun? What is it like in the space between the stars?" Voyager deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin told Space.com. "We're at a very exciting time of starting to connect what we know and what we've seen, living with this star [our sun] to what is out there.".

"What's next? Voyager is just going to keep on going. You know, people sometimes think, 'When's the mission going to end?' It's never going to end," Fox added to Space.com. "Even when we can no longer talk to Voyager, they're both going to keep going … So there's no end for the Voyager mission.".

It has been revealed that chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Referees’ chief Howard Webb has voiced his support for the decision-making behind Leny Yoro’s red card against Liverpool, despite his one-match suspension being lifted by the FA.

Yoro was sent off for fouling Alexander Isak as the Swede ran towards the goal just eight minutes into Manchester United’s 4-0 defeat to Liverpool on Sunday.

Referee Sam Barrott adjudged it to be a denial of an obvious goalscoring opportunity, but United appealed for wrongful dismissal and had their appeal upheld by the FA, meaning the French defender is free to feature in United’s home game against Brentford this Saturday.

The FA said the written reasons for removing the suspension would be published in due course.

Pro Ref’s chief refereeing officer Webb, however, backed the decision to dismiss the 21-year-old, saying the call was “certainly not clearly wrong”.

Liverpool scored their opening goal directly from the free-kick awarded for Yoro’s challenge and scored a further three without reply in a torrid start to Mauricio Pochettino’s tenure as United manager.

Webb discussed the incident with former Liverpool and United striker Michael Owen in the latest edition of Match Officials: Mic’d Up, which aired on Tuesday evening but was recorded before the FA confirmed Yoro’s suspension had been removed.

“The reason we’re talking about it is the fourth consideration (in DOGSO decisions), that’s control or likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball,” Webb mentioned.

It has been revealed that “Isak’s got control of the ball, he’s got possession, he’s got the touch, he knocks it past Yoro. He’s moving at pace at that moment and a crowd comes in and knocks him down.

“There’s a question mark I guess around whether or not he would get onto that ball before [United keeper Senne] Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

“The VAR checks to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn’t.

“I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving swiftly on towards that ball. The alternative view is tha Lammens might get there first, but I think it’s a little bit debatable. (It’s) certainly not clearly wrong.”.

VAR John Brooks was of the same opinion as he noted in the audio between him and referee Barrott: “Let’s roll it through firstly to see whether the attacker is going to get on the end of the ball.

According to recent reports, “Just roll through real speed. So, at full speed, Isak maintains his momentum and likely gets on the end of it.

“OK, certainly not clearly wrong that he doesn’t. So I think the DOGSO confirmed.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chloe Mustaki is a key figure for Carla Ward's Republic of Ireland side.

Republic of Ireland defender Chloe Mustaki has been forced to withdraw from her side's 2027 Women's World Cup play-off final against Poland next month after rupturing her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

The 31-year-old sustained the injury in action for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool in the League Cup last week.

Her club have confirmed the centre-back will miss the rest of the season and that their medical team will "determine the best course of action for her rehabilitation and recovery".

Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward said she was "absolutely devastated" for the player who will be a huge loss in the side's efforts to make it the tournament in Brazil next summer.

She added: "It is a huge blow for the entire squad because of how crucial she is to this group, both on the pitch with her consistency and leadership, and off the pitch with the incredible character and positivity she brings to the dressing room.

"This is a really difficult setback, but Chloe is loved by us all. Everyone in the squad, the staff and the association is fully behind her, and we will give her all the love and support she needs to make a full recovery.".

Ward will not call up a replacement to her squad with the 24-player panel set to gather in Dublin on Tuesday.

They will play the first leg of the play-off in Gdansk on 1 December with the return fixture at the Aviva Stadium four days later. Both games kick off at 17:00 GMT.

Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.
  • For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic.
  • Sources indicate that both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.

For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow.

Sources indicate that both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran. But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.

That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil.

In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions.

As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs.

Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, notes China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own.

"If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW.

But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter.

"The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost mentioned.

That distinction has become more key as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports.

In November, Washington confirmed Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets.

"A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said.

In a recent development, this economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently remarked the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero.

That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks.

Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating.

Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost.

But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies.

It has been revealed that A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping. China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability.

Recent findings suggest that russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation.

Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.

Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East.

"Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW.

Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran.

The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf.

Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost.

"Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he mentioned.

Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine.

Industry observers note that for Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran.

Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • There were 30 shots over the night from the English champions, only four of which were on target, and in the end their winner never came.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikel Arteta may prefer to imagine his Arsenal team as a remorseless winning machine, although on nights such as these they can still demonstrate a familiar unreliability when it comes to the main purpose of it all.

There were 30 shots over the night from the English champions, only four of which were on target, and in the end their winner never came. Even in the 95th minute, Arteta’s players were still conspiring to foul it up. This Champions League game might have been decided in Arsenal’s favour within 20 minutes. By half-time it should have been a formality. Yet, as chance after chance slipped away, there was always a possibility this would end differently.

The leaders of the Bundesliga were traumatised at times by the ferocity of the Arsenal press, and there were times when Borussia Dortmund will likely have no idea how they survived. Even so, they did just that and, liberated in the second half, Maximilian Beier scored an improbable equaliser in his team’s best period. There were still 40 minutes for Arsenal to put this one to bed and they found many ways not to do so.

Sources indicate that it was notable that the man who put Arsenal ahead in the ninth minute with a right-foot thump from space on the edge of the Dortmund box was the same striker who would miss the best chance to win it. That is the Viktor Gyokeres dilemma. In the space of a single game he can look like a potential match-winner and also the last man his manager would wish to see arriving on the end of a perfect Martin Odegaard cross.

It has been revealed that so it proved on 75 minutes when Gyokeres thrust himself at an Odegaard ball into the box that just needed guiding inside the post, yet planted it decisively wide of the mark. On the touchline Arteta tried very hard to hide his despair and failed to do so.

Recent findings suggest that it ended that way, with a heroic defensive performance from the Dortmund defence, including one memorable moment when substitute Serhou Guirassy’s determination to block a cross prompted a double ricochet off his own post. One could make the argument that there were times when it was “unbelievable”, as Arteta later stated, that the ball did not find its way in. Although there were also moments when the reasons were self-evident.

“There’s an element of luck,” the Arsenal manager remarked, “and there is an element of us finishing better.”.

In fifth place in the league phase table, dropped points at home do not carry the same jeopardy in the group stage that they once did, yet even so there was a truth for Arteta to chew upon. This is a well-honed, massive-game Arsenal Champions League side that he has built. One that reached the final last season and may well go close again, but as ever they seem to be doing so in spite of the great goalscorer that so many of their nearest rivals have at their disposal.

Arteta sounded that warning after defeat in the final in Budapest at the end of May and while changes have been made, it would be hard to argue that they have been fundamental. This was a good opponent – the leaders of the Bundesliga with many exports from English football who have been reconditioned for the German game. Those include Fábio Silva, Felix Nmecha and Jobe Bellingham who had a second-half goal narrowly disallowed for offside.

Jobe Bellingham's goal RULED OUT for offside ❌ https://t.co/yaR8EX4Gs3.

After a chastening first half in which they found themselves in the teeth of the Arsenal press, Dortmund re-emerged as a much more effective attacking force. They found a way to break the Arsenal press by targeting Christos Tzolis and the run from the teenage French defender Joane Gadou that followed was exceptional. That created the goal for Beier, one of four shots on target from Dortmund – the same number as Arsenal.

Maximilian Beier punishes Arsenal to make it 1-1 😳 https://t.co/OOUmg9JnHo.

Dortmund, managed by the West German-born Croat Niko Kovac, did not always have Arsenal’s polish in possession but they certainly had the youth in their legs to match the English champions. In defence their captain Nico Schlotterback and Waldemar Anton will not have many better games. They might have been fortunate at times but they will also point to a penalty that was not given, when Gyokeres handled in his own area at the start of the second half.

Gyokeres’ first-half goal was certainly among the best he has scored for the club, invited to shoot by a Dortmund defence that simply stood off as he reached the edge of the area. He will not catch many as full as he did this one. More of a dig than a swish but with the useful consequence of packing a lot of power and a dip that meant goalkeeper Gregor Kobel saw it but could not pick out its flight.

Sources indicate that viktor Gyökeres what a HIT! 👏🔥 https://t.co/5m6FZoE8tQ.

Asked about the later Gyokeres miss, Arteta preferred to talk about other aspects of his striker’s performance. “The way he held up the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch,” Arteta said. “There was a lot to like in that performance and that’s the Viktor that we needed.”.

Even so, there was some of the Gyokeres the Arsenal manager does not need as early as the end of the first half when he debuted a wild shot over from Noni Madueke’s pass. Arteta was without David Raya who has a shoulder injury and there were no guarantees that he will be back for the Manchester City game on Sunday.

Some good moments for young Bellingham against Myles Lewis-Skelly in the first half and then a goal disallowed after the break. That came after Beier’s equaliser when Dortmund were at their counter-attacking best. In the final stages, Arsenal pressed hard for the equaliser and although there were lots of shots it would be hard to say there were lots of chances. The one that got away was the one that fell to Gyokeres.

In a recent development, arteta would later call it “a brilliant performance”. It was hard to shake the feeling from some of the caveats he added that, like everyone else, what he really thought – above all – was that his team should have won.

The performance was superb and there is no question about that from the start to the end. We played against a really good side and the domination and threat was really impressive. The general feeling inside the dressing room is that we should reward ourselves with more.

I love the courage, the fluidity and the understanding with the players with and without the ball.

That’s what we want [to finish in the top eight]. We have a big game against Manchester City at home on Sunday so we need to recover really well, we have four days to do that and sustain that momentum the way we are playing and the win will come.

Sources indicate that I think these are the best games. I’m really looking forward to it. Two draws on the bounce now and I just desperately want to win on the weekend and I know my team-mates feel the same. We are going to do everything we have to win the three points. We’re champions, we’re at home. We have a duty to perform well at the Emirates. There are things we need to improve but all in all we are going in the right direction.

It has been revealed that I feel like the performances from us up until the last shot was incredible at times. Definitely feels like two points dropped like the other day so, having dominated so much of the game we need to take all the points.

I prefer this type of game [more open rather than against a deep defence], there are more breaks and opportunities to attack space. We it’s a low block it’s more about pass, pass, pass and wait for the right moment. I feel like we are well-suited to both types of game.

In a recent development, we could have scored in the second half. We could have won the game in many different ways. We played well and created a lot of chances, we deserved to win the game but sometimes it is like that.

Sources indicate that the most notable thing is that we create those chances and get shots on goal. For sure we will score goals when games are coming up.

But they are now four points off Real Madrid, who they play next, and more than likely PSG if they beat Roma tomorrow night.

Industry observers note that arsenal with a remarkable combination of poor finishing and bad decision-making in the final third. They ended the night with 56 touches in the Dortmund box and 29 shots, but only four of those shots were on target.

There was time for one late scramble, but at the final whistle it is the Borussia Dortmund fans celebrating the draw.

That result is going to make it very difficult for Arsenal to finish in the top two, but they will hope to have enough for a top-eight finish. They fail to win at home for the first time this season.

Dortmund had their moments, a very strong start to the second half when they could have scored more than once.

Industry observers note that but over the piece, the story is Arsenal’s profligacy. Twenty nine shots on goal and more than two expected goals, but not enough to show for it.

I’m very happy with him. He’s progressing and not only developing physically but with the ball and this is what we need.

I’m very impressed with them, with what Niko has done with the team, especially the way they are playing, the way they are dominating games, the amount of threat that they are able to create.

Sources indicate that mikel Arteta seems quite set on his left-back pecking order: Riccardo Calafiori starts on weekends, and Piero Hincapie starts in midweek. They are very different players (Calafiori is the more adventurous, while Hincapie is more of an old-school defender) and it seems that Arteta feels Hincapie is better suited to Champions League football. He’ll be tested tonight against the Bundesliga leaders.

According to recent reports, by Yannick HuberOn Tuesday, all eyes will be on Ethan Nwaneri. The Champions League clash between Arsenal and Borussia Dortmund marks the 19-year-old’s return to the club where he grew up, where he became the Premier League’s youngest player and from whom he joined Dortmund on loan in the summer. It would be hard to imagine a more poignant setting. But for Nwaneri, facing Arsenal is about more than a reunion. It is also an opportunity to finally make his mark at Dortmund.

So far his time in Germany has not gone according to plan. Nwaneri arrived with a considerable reputation and high expectations, but has become less prominent in recent weeks. His playing time has diminished and he has frequently had to settle for a place on the bench.

But there are several reasons to believe that, of all games, this meeting with his former club could give his Dortmund career fresh impetus.

Arsenal: Kepa; White, Konsa, Gabriel, Hincapie; Rice, Lewis-Skelly; Madueke, Odegaard, Tzolis; GyokeresSubs: Meslier, Porter, Saliba, Mosquera, Eze, Timber, Merino, Havertz, Calafiori, Guimaraes, Dowman.

Dortmund: Kobel, Ryerson, Anton, Schlotterbeck, Gadou, Svensson, Veerman, Nmecha, Bellingham, Beier, SilvaSubs: Drewes, Meyer, Bensebaini, Guirassy, Chukwuemeka, Nwaneri, Karetsas, Sabitzer, Mane, Albert, Dos Santos, Reggiani.

Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player the last time they played Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League, and tonight he will have to make do without first-choice goalkeeper David Raya.

Arsenal’s manager struck an upbeat note when describing the shoulder or upper arm injury Raya sustained at Newcastle, and it appears he has avoided a long-term absence.

Even two weeks out, however, would mean Raya missing Premier League fixtures against Manchester City, Brentford and Spurs – possibly Arsenal’s most testing week of the season. Arteta did not rule out a return to face City on Sunday.

Kepa Arrizabalaga is expected to deputise against Dortmund, who are top of the Bundesliga and have won three of their four Champions League league phase games. They won at the Emirates in a pre-season friendly, and Jobe Bellingham and on-loan Arsenal attacker Ethan Nwaneri are among their ranks.

These Champions League fixtures can feel secondary in importance to Premier League fare because of the competition’s new format, but a top-two finish in the league phase is a serious incentive.

As Arsenal discovered to their benefit last season when they “won” the league phase, the top two teams are rewarded with home second legs all the way to the final.

Arsenal are presently third on 10 points and face Real Madrid at the Emirates next, the team above them in second, so victory this evening is essential to set up that occasion.

Arteta has tended to make between four and six changes for these games, and Ben White, Piero Hincapie, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Christos Tzolis and Viktor Gyokeres are players pushing for starts after starting on the bench at Newcastle.

Also among the substitutes at St James’ Park was William Saliba, who is stepping up his return from a long-term back injury and could play his first minutes of the season tonight.

SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule returns to Earth from the ISS

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth.
  • Industry observers note that the robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov.
  • The freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth.

Industry observers note that the robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov. 20) at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China.

The freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at 5:03 p.m. EST (2155 GMT).

It has been revealed that the Dragon rolled out Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it was the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program.

The capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15, delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It brought a lot of stuff down to Earth, too.

Sources indicate that "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an patch on Tuesday (Nov. 17).

"The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth," they added.

Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.

It has been revealed that editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking, then again at 8:55 p.m. ET on Nov. 21 with news of splashdown.

He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mauricio Pochettino has barely unpacked his bags at Old Trafford, but it's already abundantly clear Manchester United need to back their latest head coach in January.
  • Following a disappointing start to the campaign and the arrival of a upcoming regulatory era in English football, the club’s latest financial results offer a clear picture as to how much room INEOS actually have to manoeuvre.
  • Man United’s most recent full-year accounts, covering the 12-month period to 30 June, 2026, which were published in September, paints a picture of cost-cutting paired with historically strong commercial standing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mauricio Pochettino has barely unpacked his bags at Old Trafford, but it's already abundantly clear Manchester United need to back their latest head coach in January.

Following a disappointing start to the campaign and the arrival of a upcoming regulatory era in English football, the club’s latest financial results offer a clear picture as to how much room INEOS actually have to manoeuvre.

Man United’s most recent full-year accounts, covering the 12-month period to 30 June, 2026, which were published in September, paints a picture of cost-cutting paired with historically strong commercial standing.

Despite having no European football last season, Man United posted record revenue of £677.6 million while trimming wages for a third consecutive year to £302.0m.

Although previous recruitment pushed player amortisation to £211.8m and left a net loss of £43.0m after finance costs, £47.0m in player-sale profits kept the underlying business moving forward.

Even more telling are Man United’s first-quarter results for 2026/27, released on November 19.

With Champions League football back at Old Trafford, quarterly revenue rose 4.1 per cent to £146.1m, and the club are predicted to earn £740m and £760m annually.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Quarterly player amortisation fell by almost 15 per cent following summer exits and Casemiro’s contract expiry, while another £20.7m was banked in player-disposal profits.

Sources indicate that this summer, the Premier League replaced Profitability and Sustainability Rules (PSR) with its newly introduced Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) system. Under SCR, clubs’ on-pitch spending - which comprises first-team player and head coach wages, transfer amortisation, and agent fees, while excluding non-playing staff, academy and women’s team costs - is capped at 85 per cent of football revenue plus net profit on player sales.

In a recent development, there is even a 30 per cent multi-year buffer up to a 115 per cent ‘Red Threshold’ before points deductions apply. However, because Man United are competing in the Champions League, they must simultaneously adhere to UEFA’s stricter 70 per cent squad cost limit ahead of the March 1 compliance checkpoint.

Therefore, Pochettino has far more breathing room in the transfer market than naysayers might suggest.

Taking the £750m midpoint of Man United’s expected 2026/27 revenue and adding roughly £45m - which is an average of player-trading profits over recent years - that gives an adjusted revenue figure of £795m.

Under the Premier League’s 85 per cent threshold, Man United could carry £675.8m in annual squad costs. Under UEFA’s tighter 70 per cent ceiling, their limit sits at £556.5m.

Industry observers note that remove non-playing staff from total wages and Man United’s first-team player and coaching bill sits near £255m. Add £186.4m in annualised amortisation and roughly £35m in agents’ fees, and total squad costs land around £476.4m - roughly 60 per cent of adjusted revenue.

That leaves roughly £80m in annual squad-cost headroom beneath UEFA’s 70 per cent cap - and nearly £200m domestically.

In a recent development, this means Man United could comfortably sanction £120m to £150m in winter transfer spending. That noted, their borrowing position and existing credit facility could yet prove to be a handbrake on any January rebuild, but from a purely regulatory standpoint, Man United's transfer expenditure picture is a rosy one.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Windsor Park would require 5,000 additional seats to host games at the 2035 World Cup.

The Irish Football Association's director of women's football Angela Platt noted the organisation is "still working through" intends with the Northern Ireland government to ensure there is funding available to make the necessary upgrades to Windsor Park in time for the 2035 World Cup.

It was confirmed on Monday that Northern Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales, the only bidders for the tournament in nine years' time, had been ratified as co-hosts.

Of the 19 venues proposed by the 'All Together' bid, Belfast's Windsor Park is the sole stadium in Northern Ireland, but would require an additional 5,000 seats to its current capacity of 18,500 as well as changes to the pitch and floodlights.

"We're obviously working with our government partners who've committed their support to help us do that, and we'll continue our endeavours to make sure that we work towards that," Platt told BBC NI's Stephen Watson.

"We know that the Northern Ireland Executive has given a commitment to back us and do whatever they can to support us in our endeavours to make sure we're ready for that hosting of the Women's World Cup in 2035.

"We have a few years to make sure we work through that.".

Northern Ireland was involved in a similar bid to host games at Euro 2028, but prepares for fixtures in Belfast at that tournament fell through when the government remarked it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in the required timescale.

Platt stated that "was in the past" and that the organisation were focused on the work required to avoid any repeat.

In a recent development, "We're still working towards making sure that it does happen and we're positive. We know that the work is there to make sure that it happens," she added.

"It's obviously disappointing when something that people work so hard to put together doesn't come to fruition, but certainly that's in the past for us.

"From our perspective, working for women's football, this is a great opportunity for Northern Ireland to get behind this and actually make sure that we do everything we can to host our Women's World Cup games here.".

UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms.

Plans to increase Windsor Park capacity to 23,750.

There is no guarantee that, even as co-hosts, there would an automatic qualification spot for Northern Ireland.

The side last qualified for a major tournament at Euro 2022 and Platt believes bringing the World Cup to the country has the potential to "inspire a upcoming generation".

"I think it can have a huge impact. We've always been blessed that we have had our women's team involved in the Women's Euros in 2022, and through my role, I get to visit other nations hosting tournaments such as this," she noted.

"I was in Sydney for the Women's World Cup (2023) and obviously saw the impact hosting a tournament like that had in Latest Zealand and Australia, and likewise for the Euros in England and Switzerland recently.

"That impact is significant. It's the growth of the game, it's the engagement, it's the legacy. So much positivity can come out of hosting major tournaments and we're excited to play our part in this and it can only have benefits for Northern Ireland in general.".

Unai Emery’s side won their first three games in the league phase but rather than bouncing back from a 3-0 defeat at Barcelona, they suffered another reverse in Istanbul.

Deniz Gul’s 77th minute header was the game’s first shot on target and was enough to seal all three points for the Turkish side.

With games against Paris St Germain and Borussia Dortmund to come either side of Christmas, Unai Emery’s men now have a challenge to finish in the top eight and earn a direct ticket into the knockout phase.

Sources indicate that even more worryingly, this latest loss made for six straight games without a win in all competitions, while Villa failed to register a single shot on target in the 90 minutes. their sixth consecutive defeat.

The pre-match talk was about the state of the pitch at RAMS Park, with Galatasaray playing the weekend’s league match away from the stadium in order for the surface to undergo emergency repairs.

As a result, Villa were unable to train on it ahead of the game and the pitch was plied with sand.

But the visitors initially acquitted themselves well and managed the cauldron of noise as they enjoyed a controlled start, with their best moment coming when they made a quick break down the right and the ball ended up with Johan Manzambi, but he could not get a shot away.

Galatasaray came into it as the first half progressed, but did not test Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, who will have welcomed a quiet opening after his recent troubles.

The intensity increased at the start of the second half and there were two flashpoints as tempers flared.

First, John McGinn and Aleksey Batrakov went into the book after McGinn flew into his counterpart as revenge for a heavy challenge on Alysson by former Tottenham defender Davinson Sanchez.

There was another coming together as Joao Gomes was booked for stopping Yunus Akgun’s counter-attack.

The hosts suddenly had the bit between their teeth and they pushed Villa back, with Aleksey Batrakov flashing a volley well over, before a loose ball from a corner fell to Gul, who showed bravery to head the ball home while taking a kick in the face from Nicolas Jackson.

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh stated, per Reuters.

Industry observers note that “It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”.

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.

#106037. 'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?
